description_text: The goal of this project is to develop modular systems for a classic action RPG – from inventory management and world interaction to combat and ability systems. At the same time, the prototype serves as a learning project to gain a deeper understanding of system architecture, modularity, and interaction in Unreal.
overview_text: The RPG prototype is a work in progress and is still under development. The work so far is divided into two phases: In Phase 1, the focus was on building core RPG systems such as a stat component, an inventory with interactions, and a basic combat system. In Phase 2, I am currently extending the project using the Gameplay Ability System (GAS) to represent stat and ability systems in a scalable and flexible way.
phase1_intro:
Phase 1 focused primarily on implementing the core systems of an RPG in a modular form, while at the same time gaining a better understanding of structure, architecture, and interaction in Unreal.
Part of the first phase was the implementation of a stat component, an inventory and equipment system, and an interaction system for items and objects in the world. These elements form a functional foundation and at the same time served as a learning basis to figure out which approaches work well and where improvements are still possible.
phase1_stats_text: The stat component is built modularly and can be assigned to any actor. It represents classic RPG values such as HP, Mana, Stamina, Armor, Base Damage, Crit Chance, and Crit Multiplier. Hits are calculated dynamically – taking into account armor and crits. Two variants are available for displaying these values: enemies receive a world-space health bar displayed above their heads, while the player uses a screen-space bar anchored in the UI.
phase1_inventory_text:
The inventory component is the central data source for the inventory system. Changes to the inventory are managed through events, ensuring the UI is always updated consistently, with the inventory component acting as the single source of truth.

Items in the inventory only contain references to their counterparts in the item database, which is stored in the Game Instance. This holds all relevant data (name, icon, mesh, stack size). Each item is defined as its own data asset, providing clear structure and reusability.

An additional rarity database maps different rarity levels – with color codes and (potentially) scaling values for damage or other properties.
phase1_ui_text:
All slots in the panels are based on the BaseSlot widget. This stores the central item information such as icon, stack size, or references, and also handles the fundamental interactions – like click, hover, or drag & drop. Drag-and-drop visuals are also encapsulated in this base class, ensuring consistent behavior across all panels.

Building on this, the entire UI follows the MVC principle: the model is provided by the inventory component, which manages all data. The controller is either the inventory root for the player inventory or the transfer root for external inventories, depending on context. The views consist of the various panels – inventory panel, equipment panel, and tooltip panel – which all interact consistently through the shared slot logic.
phase1_inventorypanel_text: The inventory panel is built as a classic grid, inspired by common RPG inventories. It forms the core of item management and offers all the basic interactions expected from such a system.
phase1_inventorypanel_list:
• Select items with highlighting
  • Hover highlighting and visual feedback
  • Double-click → Equip or consume
  • Right-click → Split stack
  • L → Lock item
  • CTRL+Click / CTRL+A → Multi-selection for Multi-action
  • Drag & Drop → Swap slots, move items, or drop into the world
phase1_equipment_text:
The equipment panel represents the character’s equipment and allows items to be placed into the appropriate slots via double-click or drag & drop. If a slot is already occupied, the item is automatically moved back into the inventory. To prevent misclicks, items can only be transferred back to the inventory – they cannot be dropped directly from the equipment slots.

The slots cover the typical equipment slots of an RPG:

  • Head
  • Chest
  • Hands
  • Legs
  • Boots
  • Weapon
  • Accessories
  • Weapon Upgrades
phase1_tooltip_text:
The tooltip panel is used to display detailed item information. It consolidates the most important data in one place, giving quick access to core properties. At a later stage of the project, it is planned to extend this with stat values and comparison features.

Currently displayed:

  • Icon
  • Item name
  • Rarity incl. color code
  • Description
phase1_transfer_text:
In addition to the player inventory, there is the option to open external inventories such as chests or bags. Here, the transfer root widget acts as the controller. This way, the player and external inventory are displayed side by side, and the basic interactions remain identical to those in the player inventory.

Additional features:

  • Transfer items between inventories via double-click
  • Drag & Drop between inventories
  • Transfer marked items with T
  • CTRL+A → select all items → transfer with T
  • Locked items are excluded
phase1_styling_text:
Visually, the inventory UI takes inspiration from classic RPGs. Colors and combinations can be adjusted centrally through a data asset.

Since the focus was on system logic, I created icons, names, and descriptions with the help of ChatGPT to establish a coherent medieval-fantasy atmosphere.
phase1_interaction_text: The interaction system is based on a generic interaction actor. This can be used for various objects in the world – from items to containers to doors and switches. When approaching, a symbol appears; when focusing, additional information such as name and rarity is displayed. Interactions are triggered via the F key, as is common in RPGs.
phase1_worlditems_text: Items lying on the ground can be picked up directly. When interacting, the character plays an animation, the item disappears from the world, and it is added to the inventory.
phase1_worldinventories_text: Containers such as chests or bags also use the interaction actor but rely on the transfer root. This allows the player to directly compare their inventory with that of the container and transfer items. Interactions mirror the basic functions of the player inventory, extended with transfer options.
phase1_worldinteractables_text: Doors, switches, or similar objects are also based on the same system. When approaching, a symbol is displayed; when focusing, the name of the object appears. The specific action is then triggered with the F key.
phase1_reflection_text:
Working on Phase 1 was mainly a process of learning and orientation. I analyzed existing games, tested my own ideas, and through many experiments learned what works and where I need to stay pragmatic.

Inspiration and research:
  • ARK: good handling of large item quantities, but problematic dropping
  • Dune Awakening: modern, elegant highlighting
  • Dishonored 2: minimalist interaction circles, but overloaded with “Press X” prompts
  • Elden Ring: clear slots, fast navigation, but cumbersome lists
  • Diablo & Baldur’s Gate: strong feedback on drops (color, glow, sound) and complex but readable inventories

Experimentation: I worked with widgets, world-/screen-space approaches, interactables, and even 3D effects. Some experiments were exciting, others I discarded – the important part was to explore and then pragmatically scale the scope back down.

Learnings:
  • Modularity of components in Unreal
  • Adoption of familiar UI patterns
  • Scope management and prioritization
Next steps:
  • Search and sorting functions
  • Multi-drop options
  • Optional additions: audio feedback & consistent theme

Conclusion: Especially for UI and interaction systems, it is crucial to conduct market research. Only then can you find out what truly feels good. A good UI conveys information clearly and concisely – without overloading the player. In this project, I also learned a great deal about Unreal’s technical side, building modular systems, and implementing UI/UX. These experiences form a valuable foundation for further development in Phase 2 with the Gameplay Ability System.
phase2_head: Phase 2 – Extending with the Gameplay Ability System
phase2_text:
Phase 2 is designed to integrate the Gameplay Ability System (GAS) into the prototype. The goal is to migrate the management of classic RPG stats – such as health, stamina, or mana – into GAS, creating a scalable foundation for buffs, debuffs, item effects, as well as classic RPG abilities. In this way, all mechanics that influence values or enable new actions can be represented consistently and flexibly.

Some parts of the existing stat component will be discarded or adapted in the process, as I realized during my research how powerful and central GAS will be for the ongoing development of the project. The implementation is still in progress but represents the next crucial step towards a consistent and future-proof system.
